items.body:
## Summary

On Windows, the managed app-server daemon's background updater runs every hour and pipes the PowerShell installer into `powershell.exe` via stdin + `Invoke-Expression`. McAfee Real Protect blocks that script every time as fileless malware (`Real Protect-PSFL!…`). The user then gets an antivirus alert every hour, and the daemon never updates.

This looks like the missing piece for #48528. That report found the same hourly `Real Protect-PSFL` detections and the same `powershell.exe` command line, but could not identify the parent process. On this machine the 7 detections match the 7 `installer_run` failures in `daemon-updater.stderr.log` one-to-one, with the same timestamps.

## Environment

- Windows 11 Home, 10.0.26220, x64
- Antivirus: McAfee WPS 1.40.161.1 (active). Microsoft Defender is in passive mode and reports no detections.
- Codex CLI: `codex-cli 0.162.1` (npm)
- Managed daemon: `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\packages\app-server-daemon\releases\0.162.1-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\bin\codex.exe app-server --listen unix:// --managed-daemon`
- Codex Desktop (Store) 26.1007.2314.0 was also running. Its own `codex.exe` instances are separate processes and are not involved.
- `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\app-server-daemon\settings.json` does not exist, so the default settings apply.

## What happens

1. I started the Codex CLI for the first time that day at 16:55 local time (14:55 UTC). The CLI started the managed daemon and its updater (two `codex.exe app-server` processes from the release path above).
2. From then on the updater runs once per hour. It fetches the installer, which succeeds, and then runs the installer, which fails:

```text
{"stage":"installer_fetch","outcome":"succeeded",...}
{"stage":"installer_run","outcome":"failed","failure":{"kind":"other","os_code":null}}
{"stage":"scheduled_update","outcome":"failed","failure":{"kind":"other","os_code":null}}
```

3. The installer is started with this command line. The same string is embedded in `codex.exe`, next to `failed to invoke standalone Codex updater`:

```text
powershell.exe -NoLogo -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command [Console]::OutputEncoding = [System.Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false); try { Invoke-Expression ([Console]::In.ReadToEnd()) } catch { Write-Error $_; exit 1 }
```

4. McAfee scans the stdin buffer through AMSI and blocks it. The PowerShell Operational log records event 4100:

```text
In Zeile:1 Zeichen:1
+ [CmdletBinding()]
Das Skript enthält schädliche Daten und wurde von Ihrer Antivirensoftware blockiert.
FullyQualifiedErrorId = ScriptContainedMaliciousContent,Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.InvokeExpressionCommand
```

(German locale. In English: "This script contains malicious content and has been blocked by your antivirus software.")

5. McAfee `detection.log` entry, identical every hour:

```text
target:    [memory] size: 136344 bytes, app: powershell.exe 10.0.26100.9587, backing file: ''
sensor:    IAntiMalware
detection: Real Protect-PSFL!2BF5F369F936
result:    infected
```

## Correlation (UTC, 2026-10-13)

| McAfee detection | updater `installer_run failed` |
|---|---|
| 15:00:40.868 | 15:00:41.026 |
| 16:00:44.926 | 16:00:45.282 |
| 17:00:47.408 | 17:00:47.567 |
| 18:00:49.912 | 18:00:50.057 |
| 19:00:52.726 | 19:00:52.878 |
| 20:00:56.855 | 20:00:57.163 |
| 21:01:01.590 | 21:01:02.072 |

No scheduled task or other process starts `powershell.exe` at these times.

## Additional observations

- After the CLI exits, both daemon processes keep running. I then updated the CLI via npm, and the daemon from the old release path is still running. The hourly alerts therefore continue after the user has closed Codex, and nothing on screen points to Codex as the cause. This matches the lifecycle concerns in #51961 and #48195.
- To the user, this looks like "something on my machine runs a malicious PowerShell script every hour". When they ask Codex in a session, it correctly says that none of its session processes did this, which makes the cause even harder to find.
- I did not capture the blocked script content itself. 136,344 bytes is consistent with the current `install.ps1`. #36118 shows that McAfee also blocks the official `install.ps1` (verified hash) when it is run from disk, so this is most likely a false positive on the official installer, not a tampered download.

## Expected behavior

- The background updater should not depend on a stdin `Invoke-Expression` + `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass` path. Security products classify that pattern as fileless malware. A native download, checksum verification and swap in Rust would avoid PowerShell entirely.
- If the installer run fails with `ScriptContainedMaliciousContent`, the updater should record that reason (instead of `"kind":"other"`), back off, and stop retrying every hour. Each retry raises a new AV alert.
- Closing the CLI should stop the daemon and the updater. If they must stay running, there should be a visible, documented way to opt out of daemon auto-start and auto-update.

## Related

- #48528: same hourly `Real Protect-PSFL` detections and the same command line, parent process not identified there
- #36118: McAfee blocks `install.ps1` during a manual `codex update`
- #51961, #48195: daemon and updater auto-start and persist without explicit opt-in

No antivirus settings or exclusions were changed. No raw logs, private paths or credentials are attached.

Codex repeatedly fails with `stream disconnected before completion`. Retrying has not resolved the recurring problem, interrupting requests before completion.

1. Submit a request in the Codex desktop app on Windows.
2. The request fails with the stream-disconnection error above.
3. Retry; the problem continues to recur.

This describes the observed workflow, not a deterministic minimal reproduction. The exact triggering prompt, model, reasoning effort, token usage, and context-window usage have not been collected.

Requests should finish reliably, or recover from interruptions with a clear way to continue unfinished work.

```bash
   taskset -c "$codex_cpu" codex --no-daemon
   ```

```bash

  "Reply with OK only. Do not run commands or change files."
```

The initial user thread count was approximately 74. The exact number of threads required to trigger the failure has not been determined.

### What is the expected behavior?

Expected behavior: Interactive Codex should support constrained thread budgets, ideally with a configurable worker limit and graceful fallback if worker-thread creation fails. At minimum, it should report the resource-limit failure clearly instead of remaining stuck at startup.

items.body:
## What issue are you seeing?

The native Codex app-server `plugin/list` response returns multiple remote plugin records with the same marketplace-qualified summary identity but different `remotePluginId` values. Some variants also differ in publisher and authentication policy. A consumer cannot safely treat `summary.id` plus marketplace name as a unique installation identity.

Observed on October 13, 2026 with Codex CLI/app-server **0.160.0**, on macOS ARM64. The consuming integration was OpenClaw **2026.10.2**. The collisions were verified directly in the native app-server response, independently of OpenClaw's discovery merge or installation guard. No model inference or installation was needed.

The default `plugin/list` response contained seven conflicting groups / fourteen records. For every pair:

- `summary.id` and marketplace name were identical.
- Both `remotePluginId` values were nonempty and distinct.
- Both records had remote source type and reported `availability: AVAILABLE` and `installPolicy: AVAILABLE`.
- Neither marketplace record had a local path, so these were not symlink aliases.
- The conflicts were already present in the default request, before supplemental marketplace-kind requests.

A sanitized comparison of the seven groups follows. Group labels are placeholders, not plugin names or IDs.

| Group | Distinct remote IDs | Same summary ID | Publisher differs | Authentication policy differs | Installed/enabled variants |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 2 | yes | yes | yes: ON_USE / ON_INSTALL | 1 of 2 |
| B | 2 | yes | yes | yes: ON_USE / ON_INSTALL | 0 of 2 |
| C | 2 | yes | yes | no | 0 of 2 |
| D | 2 | yes | yes | no | 0 of 2 |
| E | 2 | yes | no | no | 0 of 2 |
| F | 2 | yes | no | no | 0 of 2 |
| G | 2 | yes | no | no | 0 of 2 |

The downstream integration excludes ambiguous installation targets and reports seven identity warnings. That guard is intentional and remains enabled. Existing separately verified integrations continue to work. This report does not request weakening the guard or automatically choosing the first, newest, or installed variant.

## What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Start an authenticated owned `codex app-server` stdio connection using an account that receives remote plugin catalog entries.
2. Initialize it and send `plugin/list` with the default marketplace selection:

```json
{"id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"clientInfo":{"name":"catalog-repro","version":"1.0"},"capabilities":{"experimentalApi":true}}}
{"method":"initialized","params":{}}
{"id":2,"method":"plugin/list","params":{"cwds":["<absolute workspace path>"]}}
```

3. Group the returned plugin records by marketplace name and the exact plugin `summary.id`.
4. Within each group, compare distinct nonempty `remotePluginId` values and the corresponding publisher, version, install policy and authentication policy.
5. A group with more than one distinct remote ID reproduces the ambiguous canonical selector. In the observed response all seven pairs also had exactly identical summary IDs, not merely normalized display-name collisions.

Catalog contents are account-dependent; the exact seven-group count is the observed snapshot, not a claim that every account returns these records.

## What is the expected behavior?

Independently installable remote variants should have unique canonical identities, or superseded records should be identified unambiguously. If duplicate summary IDs are intentional, please document the stable remote-variant selector that consumers must retain across `plugin/list`, detail, installation and policy binding, including how to distinguish different publishers/authentication policies.

An installation decision must preserve the selected remote identity and its policy. A highest-version, installed-record, publisher-name or first-response heuristic is not a safe substitute for explicit selection.

## Additional information

Raw plugin/remote IDs, account details, endpoint and local paths, credentials, full catalog metadata and screenshots are intentionally omitted. The table was derived from a read-only direct native response; no plugin installation, authentication change, new user turn or external test message was performed during diagnosis. The source of the duplicate records (service response, cache, or client projection) has not been established.

I searched this repository for `remotePluginId`, `plugin/list` with duplicate, same plugin ID and ambiguous catalog reports before filing. The local-versus-remote lookup problem in #47140 appears related to identity handling but does not describe these duplicate records in the default catalog response.

2. Ask: **"Create a file named `text.txt` in my ChatGPT Library with the content `test`."**
3. Codex reports that no native Library function is available and does not create the file.
4. As a control test, Codex can create a normal file in its local project workspace.

Codex can work with local project files but has no exposed tool to create a file in ChatGPT Library in this session. Local filesystem permissions and the ChatGPT Library are distinct capabilities; increasing the filesystem sandbox permissions cannot supply an absent Library integration.

Codex should be able to, with appropriate account/workspace permissions:

6. Return a stable Library file reference usable in ChatGPT conversations and ChatGPT Work.

- Codex can retrieve an existing Library file when authorized.

- Codex CLI 0.160.0

1. A repository required every outgoing commit to reference a work item. This was visible in the repository's CI workflow and secondary agent documentation.
2. A delegated source correction passed local checks and independent exact-source review.
3. Its final commit message omitted the required work-item reference.
4. The coordinating agent pushed and opened a PR without checking the complete outgoing commit range. Native CI then rejected that commit.
5. In a separate part of the same workflow, the agent substituted a static-analysis new-code heuristic for the requested qualification semantics without resolving the operator's objection. Tests asserted the chosen wiring rather than proving the promised measurement.

items.body:
Sanitized technical reproduction only; no private repository contents, account data, credentials or machine identifiers. Prepared 13 October 2026.

## Environment

- Native Codex CLI bundled with desktop: 0.162.0-alpha.17.2, valid OpenAI OpCo signature.
- Executable SHA256: d13914ced6c7af174d8d638db938284231227312104b06a25e9608c632a7daec.
- Windows 11 Enterprise, build 26300.9550 / DisplayVersion 26H2.
- Git for Windows 2.55.0.windows.5; Python 3.13.15.

## Minimal reproduction

In a newly created disposable Git repository with a synthetic tracked text file and one local commit, run the following using the installed Codex executable and managed configuration. The repository has no remote or application files. Replace the example path with the disposable checkout. No permission changes are needed for this reproduction.

```powershell
codex -c windows.sandbox=mxc sandbox --include-managed-config --permission-profile :read-only -C C:\path\to\synthetic-repo -- python -c 'import os; print(os.getcwd()); os.chdir(".")'
codex -c windows.sandbox=mxc sandbox --include-managed-config --permission-profile :read-only -C C:\path\to\synthetic-repo -- git --no-optional-locks status --porcelain=v1
```

Observed: os.chdir produces PermissionError/WinError 5; Git exits 128 with “fatal: this operation must be run in a work tree”. Explicit `git -C` and --git-dir/--work-tree variants also fail. `git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree` returns true and `git log -1 --format=%H` succeeds. The same Python and Git checks pass outside the sandbox.

The behavior was also reproduced using app-server command/exec with sandboxPolicy `{"type":"readOnly","networkAccess":false}`, so it is not specific to shell quoting or the CLI sandbox frontend.

Direct SetCurrentDirectoryW gives WinError 5 for `.`, `.\`, trailing-backslash, forward-slash, extended-path and `\.` forms; the exact canonical absolute backslash path succeeds. Direct read/list/traverse/read-control/synchronize CreateFileW handles succeeded. These observations do not identify the internal component at fault.

## Controlled comparison and why fallback was not adopted

Process-only `windows.sandbox=elevated` comparison restores all tested directory/Git operations and runs as CodexSandboxOffline. Both modes deny create/modify/delete/rename/outside-file creation and block a tested external TCP connection. However, with the same readOnly/networkAccess:false request, elevated permits a TCP connection to an owner-controlled loopback listener while MXC denies it. Owner-positive controls confirm both endpoints were reachable before each test; no application data was sent to the external endpoint.

Thus elevated was not adopted as a transparent replacement for this installation's existing MXC boundary. Saved settings and permissions remain unchanged. This is not a general security claim about elevated mode.

## Requested investigation

Please investigate MXC strict read-only directory reacquisition/path handling on this Windows build and identify a supported correction that preserves the existing read-only and offline boundaries. Expected behavior is that normal directory navigation and read-only Git worktree inspection succeed while writes remain denied. The precise vendor component responsible is currently unknown.

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

ChatGPT desktop app in Codex mode on Windows. Computer Use plugin version 26.1007.21434.

### What feature would you like to see?

I'd like to tell Codex "quit the app" and have it perform the normal graceful Quit action through a supported first-party lifecycle tool.

Windows already has a documented Ctrl+Q Quit action, but the installed Computer Use guidance prohibits automating the ChatGPT/Codex host UI. No dedicated Quit tool is exposed in my task. I'm requesting a narrow supported capability, not removal of the general self-automation restriction or a force-kill workaround.

Expected behavior:

- An explicit quit-only request authorizes one graceful Quit of the verified official app.
- Do not treat closing a window or losing the agent connection as verified full app exit.
- Preserve a small action intent before the session ends; report an uncertain outcome honestly and avoid replaying Quit automatically.
- Leave save/discard decisions to the user, and do not broaden access to settings, chats, credentials or other host UI controls.
- Do not reopen the app unless restart was separately requested. A simple Quit request should not become an update/restart setup workflow.

### Additional information

This capability would also be a prerequisite for separately approved unattended restart/update workflows, but this request is specifically for graceful Quit.

Related reports: [#23452](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/23452) concerns host self-inspection refusal; [#38477](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/38477) concerns agents repeatedly selecting the protected host target; [#43377](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/43377) concerns SessionEnd dispatch during Windows Quit. This request concerns a deliberately scoped lifecycle operation, not a reproduction or resolution of those bugs.

References: [official app shortcuts](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/app/commands), [Computer Use documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/computer-use).

No private paths, account details, screenshots, logs or session transcripts are included.

- moving an existing chat into a project in the browser persists after refresh;
- after normal synchronization delay, those browser-originated assignments appear correctly in the Windows desktop app and continue to persist there.

This strongly narrows the failure to the **desktop-originated project-assignment write/reconciliation path**, rather than general project persistence or cross-device read synchronization.

## Environment

- Windows 11
- Current combined ChatGPT / Codex desktop application
- ChatGPT Projects + Work / local chat workflows
- Same ChatGPT account/workspace in browser and desktop
- Observed October 13, 2026

Exact current desktop package version was not collected before filing.

## Reproduction

### A. Browser-originated assignment — works

1. Open ChatGPT in a browser.
2. Create a new chat inside an existing project, or move an existing chat into that project.
3. Refresh the browser.
4. Confirm the chat remains in the project.
5. Open or return to the Windows desktop app.
6. Wait for normal synchronization.

Observed: the project placement eventually appears on desktop and appears to remain stable.

### B. Desktop-originated assignment — fails

1. Open the Windows ChatGPT/Codex desktop app.
2. Create a chat under a project, or move an existing chat into a project using the desktop UI.
3. The UI initially shows the chat under the project.
4. Continue using the app / allow synchronization to occur.

Observed: after some time, the assignment reverts and the chat leaves the project, remaining only under Recents / without the intended project association.

The failure is intermittent in timing but repeatable as a desktop-vs-browser behavioral difference.

## Expected behavior

Project membership should be durable regardless of whether it is created or changed from ChatGPT Web or the Windows desktop app.

A successful desktop move should remain associated with the selected project and survive subsequent synchronization/reconciliation.

## Why this is useful diagnostically

This comparison rules out several broader explanations:

- Project membership itself can persist on the account.
- Browser writes persist across refresh.
- Desktop can receive and display browser-originated project membership.
- Cross-device synchronization from browser -> desktop works.

The remaining suspect area is therefore the desktop write path, its local project/thread metadata, or a later reconciliation step that overwrites/ignores a desktop-originated assignment.

Potential cases to distinguish:

1. Desktop UI updates optimistically, but the membership mutation is never durably saved.
2. The write succeeds, but a later desktop reconciliation restores stale local metadata.
3. Desktop and server use different membership records and the desktop path updates only one of them.
4. A successful mutation acknowledgement is returned before durable persistence is complete.

## Related issues

- #53486 — project membership differs between sidebar and thread metadata; successful move not reflected in readback (macOS)
- #42215 — Windows Work/project context failures, including stale project state and project sync problems

This report is intentionally separate because the browser-vs-desktop persistence comparison on Windows is a clean reproduction boundary and may help isolate the write/reconciliation layer.

## Additional context

The same Windows installation has also previously exhibited a separate issue where **New chat** retained an incompatible previously selected project and Work showed `Could not use this project for a local chat`. A prior state-level recovery regenerated `.codex-global-state.json`, but that earlier workaround is **not being claimed as a fix for this project-membership persistence problem**.

No project mirrors, local databases, credentials, or working files were deleted while establishing this reproduction.

Private project names, chat titles, account identifiers, and filesystem paths are omitted.

items.body:
### Summary

GPT-5.6 Sol is also experiencing intermittent response-stream failures in a native Codex app-server integration. In one retained turn, app-server emitted a complete `agentMessage` through `item/completed` with `phase: "final_answer"`, then emitted five retryable stream-disconnect errors and finally `turn/completed` with `status: "failed"`.

This is based on read-only inspection of the actual JSON-RPC event stream, not on the assistant saying that it had replied.

### Environment

- Actual executable version: `codex-cli 0.146.0`, read from the running container.
- Model and effort from the actual `turn/start` request: `gpt-5.6-sol`, `xhigh`.
- Linux x86_64; Docker; custom Telegram conversation gateway.
- Codex integration: native `codex app-server`, connected to the gateway over **stdio JSON-RPC**.
- ChatGPT sign-in / OAuth authentication.
- Observation date: October 13, 2026 UTC (October 14, UTC+08:00).
- This deployment is on an older CLI version. **I have not reproduced this on the latest release.** Please indicate if a subsequent release fixes this specific failure sequence.

The stdio transport above is the gateway-to-app-server connection. It does not establish whether the upstream model request used WebSocket or HTTP/SSE; that upstream transport was not captured in this audit.

### Representative event ordering

All times below are **UTC on October 13, 2026**, from the same thread and turn. Thread, turn and item identifiers and message bodies are omitted.

| Timestamp | Native app-server notification | Recorded fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 19:46:12.602 | `turn/started` | `status: "inProgress"` |
| 19:46:35.388 | `item/completed` | `type: "agentMessage"`, `phase: "commentary"`, 262 Unicode code points |
| 19:48:36.454 | `item/completed` | `type: "agentMessage"`, `phase: "final_answer"`, 3,669 Unicode code points |
| 19:48:39.480 | `error` | `willRetry: true`, `responseStreamDisconnected`, `httpStatusCode: null` |
| 19:48:42.617 | `error` | same retryable error, retry 2/5 |
| 19:48:46.563 | `error` | same retryable error, retry 3/5 |
| 19:48:50.681 | `error` | same retryable error, retry 4/5 |
| 19:48:55.437 | `error` | same retryable error, retry 5/5 |
| 19:49:01.639 | `error` | `willRetry: false`, `codexErrorInfo: "other"` |
| 19:49:01.640 | `turn/completed` | `status: "failed"`, `error.codexErrorInfo: "other"` |

The first retryable error arrived **3.026 seconds after** the completed final-answer item. The failed terminal notification arrived **25.186 seconds after** that item.

Representative retry error, with identity fields omitted:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "message": "Reconnecting... 1/5",
    "codexErrorInfo": {
      "responseStreamDisconnected": {
        "httpStatusCode": null
      }
    }
  },
  "willRetry": true
}
```

The terminal error was:

```text
stream disconnected before completion: An error occurred while processing your request. You can retry your request, or contact us through our help center at help.openai.com if the error persists. Please include the request ID [retained privately] in your message.
```

A final-answer item completing is not equivalent to the turn completing; this report does **not** assert that the two protocol events must have identical status. The investigation request is why the upstream request continues into repeated processing/stream errors after a complete final-answer item, and what integrations should do with that already-completed output.

### Other failures and intermittent recovery

A selected sample of the most recent **10 user-triggered turns**, frozen at 20:06:36 UTC, contained 7 completed and 3 failed turns. Autonomous/system-triggered turns were excluded from this count. This is a small diagnostic sample, not a population failure-rate estimate.

| Turn started (UTC) | Terminal failure (UTC) | Completed assistant output before failure | Retry notifications |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| 19:45:19.302 | 19:45:44.502 | No completed agent-message item | 5 |
| 19:46:12.602 | 19:49:01.640 | Commentary + complete final-answer item, as above | 5 |
| 20:03:08.581 | 20:03:36.262 | No completed agent-message item | 5 |

There were also recovered retries: the turn starting at 19:58:03.577 produced three retry notifications and ultimately completed at 19:58:43.892. Thus retry notifications are not being counted as separate failed turns, and the same native thread is not uniformly failing on every request.

### User impact and integration boundary

The gateway successfully delivered the earlier commentary. Its current integration buffers final-answer items until the native turn reaches `status: "completed"`. When this turn instead reached `failed`, the gateway discarded the buffered final-answer text, so the user received an error rather than the already-generated reply.

That discard policy is **our downstream integration behavior**, not a claim that Codex itself deleted the response. It explains the user-visible missing reply, but it does not explain the upstream errors or the native failed-turn outcome.

During the audited interval, the gateway remained running/healthy with no container restart, and its Telegram transport recorded no `delivery_failed` events. This narrows the observed failure stage; it does not prove the underlying model-network path was healthy. Successful later replies received Bot API confirmations, which do not imply the user read them.

### Observed reproduction and limitations

1. Continue an existing conversation using native app-server with `gpt-5.6-sol` and `xhigh`.
2. Intermittently observe repeated `Reconnecting... 1/5` through `5/5` errors.
3. Some turns recover; others terminate with the generic request-processing error.
4. In the representative turn, a completed `final_answer` item was already present before the retries and failed terminal status.

This is an observed sequence in a retained conversation, **not a deterministic minimal public reproducer**. No controlled fresh-thread, alternate-model, latest-version, network-route or upstream raw-SSE comparison has been performed. The app-server error projection exposes `responseStreamDisconnected` and later `other`; it is insufficient to distinguish a physical transport interruption, an upstream error returned within the response stream, or a client-side processing issue. No explicit quota-exhaustion or context-window-exceeded error is present in the selected failures.

### Questions for maintainers / expected behavior

- Can request diagnostics explain the sequence `item/completed(final_answer)` -> repeated `responseStreamDisconnected` -> `turn/completed(failed)` for GPT-5.6 Sol?
- Is this a known issue in app-server 0.146.0, and is there a specific fixed release?
- Can the terminal error preserve a more actionable classification than `other`, and clarify whether an already-completed final-answer item remains deliverable after a failed turn?
- What supported recovery procedure preserves the existing conversation and completed output without blindly replaying an input or previously executed tools?

Expected: reliable successful turn termination, or an actionable interruption/recovery path with clear semantics for completed output.

Possibly related symptom reports: #52919, #53484. These are related references, **not evidence of a shared root cause**.

### Privacy

Request IDs and original events are retained privately for appropriate support correlation. No credentials, chat content, raw logs, internal paths, account details or thread/turn identifiers are attached to this public issue.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Installed Windows package `OpenAI.Codex`: **26.1007.2314.0**, verified with `Get-AppxPackage`. The About dialog was not captured.

### What subscription do you have?

Not captured. This occurred in a signed-in local Codex desktop chat.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows x64; PowerShell reports `Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0`.

### What issue are you seeing?

A private PR review successfully began and returned a pinned snapshot, but the single fresh reviewer subagent remained `pending_init` through repeated waits. It never returned a progress update, a completed review, or a failure. After the coordinator interrupted the stalled child, the private review tool rejected the attempt to record a failed outcome with only:

```text
The plugin did not accept this review.
```

Consequently, no review report was produced and saving the failed outcome was not confirmed. The persisted run state after rejection was not independently inspected.

This was observed on **2026-10-13** in the Codex desktop private Code Review workflow for the public PR https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/pull/19114. It is a Codex workflow failure; no defect in the reviewed PR is being asserted.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

The following is the observed sequence from one attempt, not a confirmed deterministic reproducer:

1. Open a PR-specific review chat and request a private, read-only review using exactly one fresh child with `fork_turns: "none"`. Instruct the coordinator not to inspect code itself, and prohibit code changes or external posting.
2. Call `mcp__codex_app__record_private_review` with `action: "begin"` and this request:

   ```json
   {
     "account": {"hostId": "local", "hostname": "github.com", "login": "piotrnowakowski"},
     "pullRequest": {"hostname": "github.com", "number": 19114, "owner": "pingdotgg", "repository": "t3code"}
   }
   ```

   This succeeded and returned run ID `aa6f1873-abf8-463b-82c2-1f6f8df463e3`, base/merge-base `8ac4b97dae6bff7258fa5091a908116902fbd635`, head `7d7099cca29b86115f11dededc0185c00898b301`, and the review criteria/result schema.

3. Call `collaboration.spawn_agent` exactly once with task name `pr_review_aa6f1873`, `fork_turns: "none"`, and the snapshot plus read-only execution instructions. Do not override its model or reasoning settings. The tool returned:

   ```json
   {"task_name": "/root/pr_review_aa6f1873"}
   ```

4. Wait for that same child using `collaboration.wait_agent`, repeatedly with 10- or 50-second timeouts. One wait returned `aborted`; subsequent waits repeatedly returned:

   ```json
   {"message": "Wait timed out.", "timed_out": true}
   ```

   A queue-only `collaboration.send_message` asking the same reviewer for progress was accepted, but no reply arrived. No replacement or parallel reviewer was spawned.

5. On two later checks, call `collaboration.list_agents` with `path_prefix: "/root/pr_review_aa6f1873"`. Both returned:

   ```json
   {"agents": [{"agent_name": "/root/pr_review_aa6f1873", "agent_status": "pending_init"}]}
   ```

6. Interrupt the stalled reviewer with `collaboration.interrupt_agent`. It returned:

   ```json
   {"previous_status": "pending_init"}
   ```

7. Call `mcp__codex_app__record_private_review` with the successful begin's run ID and a failed outcome:

   ```json
   {
     "action": "finish",
     "runId": "aa6f1873-abf8-463b-82c2-1f6f8df463e3",
     "outcome": {
       "type": "failed",
       "error": "Fresh reviewer pr_review_aa6f1873 remained pending_init throughout repeated waits and status checks, never initialized, and produced no review report. The stalled reviewer was interrupted. No code was inspected by the coordinating agent and no findings are available."
     }
   }
   ```

   The tool returned:

   ```json
   {
     "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "The plugin did not accept this review."}],
     "isError": true
   }
   ```

### What is the expected behavior?

- An accepted fresh reviewer should initialize, or return an actionable startup failure instead of remaining indefinitely opaque as `pending_init`.
- The private review workflow should accept a failed outcome for a valid run when its reviewer cannot start, or explain the specific rejection and recovery action.
- The user should have a verifiable terminal failed/cancelled run state even when no findings can be produced.

### Additional information

- The coordinator did not inspect the PR's code, change code, or post anything externally during the failed review.
- The child never supplied its own outcome; the `finish` failure text described the coordinator's observed startup stall and interruption. Whether the plugin rejected that lifecycle state, the failed outcome, or another condition is unknown.
- The available instruction stated four concurrency slots including the coordinator. Only one child was created in this attempt. Internal scheduler occupancy was not inspected.
- The initial startup cause and any relationship to the aborted wait or later progress message are unverified. There was no source-level diagnosis or retry with a replacement child.
- Related: #49986 describes a completed agent becoming `pending_init` after queue-only mail. This attempt concerns a fresh reviewer that produced no completed turn, plus rejection of a private review failure outcome; a shared root cause is not established.
- No credentials, private source code, or full session archives are attached. Run/task identifiers and the public PR are included for correlation.

# [Bug] Excessive initial context (~273k tokens) and 24M-token consumption in Codex Desktop with a custom Responses provider and subagents

## Summary

On October 13, 2026, Codex Desktop for Windows consumed approximately **24 million tokens** through a custom OpenAI-compatible Responses API provider (Xiaomi MiMo-v2.6-pro) during a multi-agent software-development workflow.

The local logs show:

1. **Large initial input:** the first recorded model response in four Desktop sessions had approximately **273,000 input tokens**. The first CLI diagnostic response had **105,500 input tokens**.
2. **Full history inheritance:** three subagents were spawned from one parent with `fork_turns = all`.
3. **Low cache reuse:** approximately **81.9% of the locally recorded input tokens** were cache misses.

I am reporting this to understand whether the context size is expected, whether the Codex runtime can reduce it, and how to use multi-agent workflows with custom Responses providers without unexpectedly high usage. The provider-side caching behavior has not been independently diagnosed.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11, build 26200
- Codex CLI: `0.157.1`; Codex Desktop for Windows
- Execution: native Windows / PowerShell
- Model: `mimo-v2.6-pro`
- Custom provider: Xiaomi MiMo Token Plan (Singapore), `wire_api = "responses"`
- Model configuration: `model_context_window = 1048576`, `model_reasoning_effort = "high"`
- Desktop: plugins enabled, including Browser, Computer Use, Chrome, Documents, PDF, Spreadsheets, and Presentations
- MCP servers configured: `node_repl`, `rea`

The provider was successfully authenticated and could call PowerShell tools from Codex CLI. No API keys or sensitive configuration values are included here.

## Actual behavior

### 1. Large initial input

The first recorded `last_token_usage.input_tokens` for each session was:

| Session start (local time) | Origin | First input tokens |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| 20:15:58 | Codex CLI diagnostic | 105,500 |
| 20:19:54 | Codex Desktop parent | 272,511 |
| 20:49:11 | Codex Desktop subagent | 272,987 |
| 20:50:05 | Codex Desktop subagent | 272,957 |
| 20:51:48 | Codex Desktop subagent | 272,972 |

The four Desktop sessions are within **476 tokens** of each other (about **0.17%** of their input size). This strongly suggests a common context component, but it does **not** establish which part came from system instructions, tool definitions, plugins, conversation history, or application state.

The simple CLI task, "Identify the operating system and current directory," eventually reported **620,765 tokens** across its session (620,251 input, none cached; 514 output), despite returning just a short answer.

### 2. One parent spawned three subagents

Parent session ID: `01a13647-2344-7be0-9f52-8d192290972b`

| Subagent | Task | `fork_turns` | Total tokens |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| Ampere | `phase1_manifest` | `all` | 3,613,046 |
| Dalton | `phase1_provenance` | `all` | 4,038,318 |
| Sagan | `phase1_unknowns` | `all` | 3,405,538 |
| **Subagents total** | | | **11,056,902** |

Each child session includes a `parent_thread_id` matching the parent, and the parent's `spawn_agent` tool-call arguments specify `fork_turns = all` for all three. Subagents were launched automatically as part of the parent workflow, rather than as three separately initiated top-level tasks.

### 3. Session token accounting

The following figures come from the **last cumulative `token_count` entry per session** in local Codex JSONL logs; they are not a request-by-request billing export:

| Session | Cache miss | Cache hit | Output | Total |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| CLI diagnostic | 620,251 | 0 | 514 | 620,765 |
| Desktop parent | 9,579,884 | 2,825,216 | 42,953 | 12,448,053 |
| Subagent Ampere | 3,302,735 | 294,144 | 16,167 | 3,613,046 |
| Subagent Dalton | 3,347,190 | 672,640 | 18,488 | 4,038,318 |
| Subagent Sagan | 2,830,266 | 560,000 | 15,272 | 3,405,538 |
| **Total** | **19,680,326** | **4,352,000** | **93,394** | **24,125,720** |

Xiaomi's dashboard for October 13, 2026 reported:

| Metric | Tokens |
| --- | ---: |
| Total | 24,360,653 |
| Input (cache miss) | 19,829,403 |
| Input (cache hit) | 4,441,344 |
| Output | 89,906 |

The local total is approximately 99.0% of the dashboard total. The figures do not match exactly, potentially due to reporting windows or differences between client and server counters. I am not asserting a billing error based on that discrepancy.

### 4. Repeated large input and limited cache hits

Analysis found **73 positive changes** in cumulative usage counters across the five sessions. These counter updates are **not necessarily equivalent to 73 individual HTTP requests**.

Examples of reported usage increments:

| Session | Input tokens | Cache miss | Cache hit |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Desktop parent | 369,379 | 318,947 | 50,432 |
| Desktop parent | 315,561 | 314,281 | 1,280 |
| Subagent Sagan | 327,114 | 314,186 | 12,928 |
| Subagent Dalton | 322,497 | 309,569 | 12,928 |
| Subagent Ampere | 332,659 | 300,403 | 32,256 |

The largest recorded `last_token_usage.input_tokens` was **422,069**. The high cache-miss fraction could reflect changes in the prompt prefix, behavior of the upstream caching implementation, or other factors; the available local logs do not isolate the cause.

## Reproduction context

This is an incident report, **not yet a minimal deterministic reproduction**:

1. Install Codex Desktop and CLI `0.157.1` on Windows.
2. Configure a custom OpenAI-compatible Responses provider using a suitable model catalog.
3. Enable Desktop plugins and MCP integrations.
4. Run a multi-agent project task and allow the parent to spawn subagents with `fork_turns = all`.
5. Inspect the first `token_count` usage entry and subsequent usage increments in `~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl`.
6. Compare input sizes and cached-input ratios for parent and subagents.

## Expected behavior / questions for maintainers

- Is a **~273k-token first input** expected for Codex Desktop with these plugins and MCP servers enabled?
- Can the Codex runtime expose a breakdown of input context size (base instructions, tool schemas, plugins, conversation history, etc.)?
- Is the **~105k CLI vs ~273k Desktop** first-input difference expected?
- Is `fork_turns = all` intended as the default for Multi-Agent V2? Can users configure a default inheritance policy while retaining functional task handoff?
- Are there known prompt caching limitations with custom Responses providers? Can Codex keep the reusable prefix stable where possible?
- Is there a supported per-session/per-agent token budget, warning threshold, or cancellation mechanism that can prevent unexpectedly large usage for third-party-billed APIs?

## Impact

A single multi-agent development workflow consumed a substantial fraction of a paid monthly Token Plan subscription. Disabling subagents entirely is not a viable long-term workaround: they are central to this workflow. I am looking for a way to preserve useful multi-agent execution while controlling unnecessary context duplication and unexpected cost.

## Diagnostics / privacy

I can provide a redacted session usage CSV, parent-child metadata, `spawn_agent` arguments, and a usage dashboard screenshot. I am not posting complete session JSONL files because they may contain private project content, local file paths, and sensitive prompts. No API credentials will be shared.

## Follow-up: cross-provider cache statistics and confirmed subagent provenance

I gathered additional evidence after filing the issue. This analysis reads existing local Codex JSONL files only; **no new MiMo API tests were performed**.

### 1. Cross-provider cache comparison

I ran `ccusage` against the local Codex rollout data and reconciled its MiMo figures with my earlier PowerShell extraction of the last cumulative `token_count` value per session.

| Metric | OpenAI models (`gpt-6.1-sol`, `gpt-5.6-luna`) | Xiaomi `mimo-v2.6-pro` |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Uncached input | 2,565,835 | 19,680,326 |
| Cached input | 80,042,368 | 4,352,000 |
| Total input | 82,608,203 | 24,032,326 |
| **Cached share of input** | **96.9%** | **18.1%** |
| Output (reasoning included) | 304,915 | 93,394 |
| Total tokens | 82,913,118 | 24,125,720 |

In this report, `Input` refers to uncached input; `Cache Read` is separate; `Reasoning` is a subset of `Output`, not an additional amount.

**Important limitation:** these were not matched tasks under identical conditions. Session history, model, workload and possibly enabled tools differed. These numbers confirm a large *observed* cache-efficiency disparity but do not establish whether it originates in Codex's request/prefix construction, the provider's cache semantics, or some combination.

### 2. Subagent provenance is confirmed

The Codex Desktop parent session `01a13647-2344-7be0-9f52-8d192290972b` spawned three children (`phase1_manifest`, `phase1_provenance`, `phase1_unknowns`). Their session metadata all contains the parent's `parent_thread_id`; the parent's `spawn_agent` calls explicitly specify `fork_turns = all` for each child.

These children together accounted for **11,056,902 tokens**. This establishes full-history inheritance at spawn time, not the precise token composition of each API request.

### 3. The initial-context question remains open

The first recorded input was **105,500 tokens** in a CLI diagnostic and **272,511–272,987 tokens** in four Desktop/child sessions. The Desktop values differ by just 476 tokens. This suggests a substantial shared context component, but I cannot isolate its origin (base instructions, tools/plugin schemas, `AGENTS.md`, inherited conversation history, etc.) from the current local counters.

### Specific requests to maintainers

1. Is there a supported way to inspect **per-component token counts for the initial request** (instructions, tool schemas, MCP/plugin contributions, conversation history)?
2. For custom Responses providers, does Codex send and preserve a `prompt_cache_key` or equivalent reusable prefix? Are there known provider compatibility requirements or limitations?
3. Can subagents be given a **default, bounded `fork_turns` policy** with reliable task handoff, while retaining multi-agent functionality?
4. Is there a supported **hard cap on input tokens, cumulative session usage or agent-tree usage**, including a way to stop parent and child requests before exceeding the limit?

My objective is not to disable subagents: they are required for the development workflow. I am looking for a supported way to keep multi-agent execution while making context size and consumption predictable. I am not attaching raw rollout JSONL files because they may expose private prompts, paths and project content; I can provide suitably redacted diagnostics if requested.

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

App

### What feature would you like to see?

Feature Request: Owner Verification for High-Impact AI Actions

Category: Security / Safety / Enhancement

Summary

Introduce an optional, user-configurable security failsafe requiring additional owner authentication before Codex executes unusually consequential, destructive, or irreversible actions.

The purpose is to protect users against accidental instructions, unauthorised access, and requests made by someone other than the legitimate account owner.

The problem

AI agents increasingly have access to substantial amounts of personally valuable work, including software projects, documents, repositories, and connected services.

Currently, an agent may receive a technically valid instruction without being able to establish whether the person issuing it is authorised to make that particular decision.

For example:

I might spend weeks developing a software project using Codex. My child could access my unlocked computer and instruct Codex to delete the entire project. Alternatively, somebody who gained unauthorised access to my session could issue the same instruction.

Neither request is inherently malicious from the AI's perspective. Both could be devastating to the legitimate owner.

A conventional "Are you sure?" confirmation is insufficient because the unauthorised person can simply confirm the action.

Access to an AI session should not automatically grant unrestricted authority over everything that AI can access.

Proposed solution

Introduce an optional High-Impact Action Protection setting.

When enabled, Codex would identify actions with unusually significant consequences and require separate owner verification before proceeding.

Examples include:

- Deleting entire projects or substantial directories.
- Permanently removing files, repositories, or backups.
- Overwriting large amounts of existing work.
- Executing unusually destructive commands.
- Making irreversible changes to important connected resources.
- Performing actions that substantially exceed the scope of ordinary project maintenance.

Verification could use a dedicated security PIN, biometric authentication, or approval through a separately authenticated trusted device.

Important design considerations

1. Independent enforcement: Authentication must be handled outside the AI agent's control. The agent must not be able to read, modify, or bypass the security mechanism.

2. User-defined protection: Users should be able to designate particularly important projects, folders, and resources as protected.

3. Context-aware detection: The system should consider the scale, reversibility, and unusual nature of an action, rather than relying solely on a list of dangerous commands.

4. Protection against indirect actions: The failsafe should cover destructive consequences achieved through scripts, tools, or sequences of individually harmless commands.

5. Minimal disruption: Routine coding, file editing, and normal development tasks should continue without repeated authentication.

6. Explicit owner approval: High-impact actions should remain blocked until independently authorised, rather than being approved through ordinary conversational confirmation.

Why this matters

As AI agents become increasingly autonomous and capable of controlling files, applications, accounts, and services, the distinction between receiving an instruction and having authority to execute it becomes critical.

This is not simply a question of preventing malicious AI behaviour. It is about protecting users from otherwise obedient AI systems carrying out devastating instructions from the wrong person.

The same principle could eventually apply across OpenAI's wider agent ecosystem.

Requested outcome

An optional, simple-to-enable security feature that protects personally valuable work and requires genuine owner verification before an AI agent can perform high-impact actions.

The goal is straightforward:

An AI should be able to help manage everything important to its user without automatically having unrestricted permission to destroy it.

Run two separate copies of codex-rs on separate machines / sandboxes that don't talk to each other.  Ask one to create a Page.  Ask the other one to enumerate Pages and read the contents.

Either there should be permission prompts at both the sign-in level and the tool call level or an instance of codex-rs should only be able to list and read pages that it created.

items.title: app-server: expose native-resolved usable context window before turn assembly

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: context
labels.description: Issues related to context management (including compaction)

labels.name: app-server

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

`codex app-server`, Codex 0.159.1, consumed by OpenClaw's native Codex integration on Linux.

Source inspection is pinned to [`rust-v0.159.1`, commit `8e68a98ef03cdde76d2e6800791ebdf1b3b95b24`](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/8e68a98ef03cdde76d2e6800791ebdf1b3b95b24). The six files linked below were independently compared with the public commit and matched. This report describes a protocol/source gap, not a newly executed inference test or a claim about every newer release.

### What feature would you like to see?

**Expose the selected model's native-resolved usable context window to app-server clients before they assemble or submit a turn, without requiring a calibration model call.**

An external context engine must decide how much history to retain before submitting input. Codex already resolves the model-specific window and usable percentage internally, but the inspected public API does not expose that resolved value at the point the client needs it.

This matters for cold starts, resumes, and model changes. A raw configured window can exceed the selected model's native maximum; a previous turn's usage notification can describe a different, larger model. Guessing a fixed percentage or reusing either number can oversize a smaller-model attempt. Always choosing anarbitrarily small fallback unnecessarily discards available history instead.

#### How to inspect the gap without running inference

1. Initialize an app-server client and inspect `model/list` and `config/read`.
2. Select a model/provider through `thread/start`, or resume a thread with the intended selection. Inspect the response before sending `turn/start`.
3. Inspect the settings update response/notification when changing the selected model. There is no resolved context-window field in the inspected contracts.
4. Compare the available values with native `with_config_overrides` and `ModelInfo::usable_context_window`, below. `config/read` exposes the authored window, not the result of that resolution.
5. For a resumed thread, note that a restored `thread/tokenUsage/updated` notification is explicitly historical replay. Its window is not evidence of the newly selected model's current allowance.

These are protocol-inspection steps, not a claim that a model-switch inference experiment was performed for this report.

#### Source evidence

- [Native configuration overrides](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/8e68a98ef03cdde76d2e6800791ebdf1b3b95b24/codex-rs/models-manager/src/model_info.rs#L19): an authored `model_context_window` is clamped to the selected model's `max_context_window` when present.
- [Native resolved and usable windows](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/8e68a98ef03cdde76d2e6800791ebdf1b3b95b24/codex-rs/protocol/src/openai_models.rs#L514): `usable_context_window` applies that model's `effective_context_window_percent`. The default is 95, but it is a model field, not a universally safe client constant.
- [`model/list` model contract](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/8e68a98ef03cdde76d2e6800791ebdf1b3b95b24/codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/model.rs#L119): no raw/resolved/usable context-window metadata.
- [`config/read` configuration](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/8e68a98ef03cdde76d2e6800791ebdf1b3b95b24/codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/config.rs#L281): authored `model_context_window`, not a selected-model resolved usable value.
- [Thread lifecycle/settings contracts](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/8e68a98ef03cdde76d2e6800791ebdf1b3b95b24/codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/thread.rs#L188): start/resume/settings/read do not provide the needed resolved value.
- [Restored token-usage notification](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/8e68a98ef03cdde76d2e6800791ebdf1b3b95b24/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/token_usage_replay.rs#L29): explicitly lifecycle replay of the persisted usage snapshot, not a new model event.

#### Requested contract

The exact API shape is up to maintainers. An additive lifecycle/settings field or a read-only resolution request would work if it:

- Resolves the actual selected model/provider and effective native configuration, including window overrides, model maximum and model-specific usable percentage.
- Is available before prompt/history assembly and without starting an inference turn.

## Summary

In ChatGPT Dots' cloud computer, files downloaded through the managed cloud browser are exposed under `/opt/codex/downloads`.

This location is mounted read-only in the agent's command execution environment.

The agent can access the downloaded file but cannot delete it. No supported file-management or download-destination configuration mechanism has been identified.

It is currently unknown whether `/opt/codex/downloads` is Chrome's actual download directory or a separate location used by the cloud browser tool to expose downloaded files.

## Environment

- Product: ChatGPT Dots
- Host: OpenAI-managed Linux cloud computer
- OS: Debian GNU/Linux 13.6 (trixie)
- Kernel: Linux 6.18.44, x86_64
- Filesystem: OverlayFS
- Download source: Google Drive via managed cloud browser

## Steps to reproduce

1. Use the Dot's managed cloud browser to download an MP4 file from Google Drive.
2. Obtain the resulting file path under `/opt/codex/downloads/<UUID>/<UUID>`.
3. Verify that the file exists and is readable.
4. Inspect the filesystem mount using `findmnt`.
5. Attempt to remove the file using `rm`.
6. Observe the `Read-only file system` error.

## Verified observations

- Downloaded file size: 176,214,009 bytes
- Device: 27
- Inode: 1050193
- `/opt`: OverlayFS, mounted read-only
- Current workspace: writable
- `/tmp`: writable
- `/home/agent`: read-only tmpfs

Deletion failed, and the downloaded file remains present.

No remounting, privilege escalation, destructive cleanup, or filesystem configuration changes were performed.

## Browser configuration limitations

Attempts to inspect `chrome://downloads` were blocked because the managed browser tool accepts only HTTP and HTTPS URLs.

The available tools do not expose an operation for reading or changing Chrome's download-directory configuration or managed browser policies.

Therefore, the following remain unverified:

- Chrome's actual download directory
- Whether Chrome policy enforces that directory
- Whether `/opt/codex/downloads` is the browser's original storage location or a separate file-exposure mechanism

## Expected behavior

Users and agents should have a supported way to:

1. Delete individual downloaded files.
2. Manage temporary files without resetting the Dot.
3. Configure a writable download destination when supported.
4. Understand download retention and storage accounting.

## Actual behavior

Downloaded files are accessible through a read-only filesystem location.

Deletion through ordinary filesystem operations fails.

No supported deletion or destination-management mechanism has been identified in the available cloud browser tools.

## Impact

Large downloads can leave files that the agent cannot remove.

The affected test file is approximately 176 MB.

Whether these files count against the Dot's writable storage quota, and how long they persist, remains unknown.

## Requested investigation

1. Clarify the relationship between the managed browser's download storage and `/opt/codex/downloads`.
2. Provide a supported mechanism for deleting individual downloaded files.
3. Explain why downloaded files are exposed through a read-only mount.
4. Document retention periods and automatic cleanup behavior.
5. Clarify storage quota accounting for these files.
6. Consider allowing downloads to be saved directly into an agent-writable workspace.

## Privacy

Original file names, full UUID paths, account identifiers, and private Google Drive information have been omitted from this public report.

Additional diagnostic details can be provided privately if required.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1007.21434, build 13901, production channel, as returned by the app update checker. The checker reported no eligible update during this investigation.

### What subscription do you have?

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0 x64.

### What issue are you seeing?

The Windows desktop app repeatedly draws attention at intermediate turn boundaries while autonomous build tasks continue working and need no user action. The user initially reported this across three active tasks, then specifically identified an in-app banner or unread indicator and attention on the Windows taskbar icon. The taskbar indicator type (badge versus flashing) was not independently captured.

Please provide a complete, supported fix covering all four surfaces together: in-app banners, unread indicators, taskbar icon attention/badges, and native desktop notifications. Merely hiding the final message or suppressing a native toast does not solve the remaining attention signals.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed workflow; this is not yet a deterministic minimal reproduction:

1. Run an autonomous multi-turn build with an active Goal, allowing it to continue without user intervention.
2. Keep genuine completion, question and permission notifications enabled.
3. Let it cross routine intermediate turn boundaries while its overall task remains unfinished and no user input is required.
4. Observe the sidebar/in-app attention and Windows taskbar, as well as native notifications, while the task continues.

During investigation, a client-recognised quiet-completion marker (`::SKIP_COMPLETION::`, the entire final message) was used as a partial workaround. It was confirmed in two completed turns on 2026-10-13 at 16:54:15 UTC and 17:00:16 UTC. The user nevertheless reported another in-app/taskbar alert. The owner had followed the workaround correctly; this was not merely an instruction-adoption failure.

Subsequent readback showed the task active with no pending input flags and no unread flag at that later instant. No matching native notification entry was found for these two quiet turns. Therefore the latest recurrence is evidence of the reported in-app/taskbar symptom, not proof that all four surfaces fired simultaneously. The precise transient state when the indicator appeared was not captured.

### What is the expected behavior?

Please add or repair a supported "actual completion or needs my input only" notification mode, applied consistently across all four surfaces.

Acceptance criteria:

- Routine progress, automatically repaired failures, healthy internal waits and automatic continuation boundaries produce no new banner, unread indicator, taskbar attention/badge, or desktop toast.
- Actual completion of the requested task/outcome still alerts the user, subject to their normal focus and notification preferences.
- Genuine questions, permission requests, blockers requiring user action, and actionable critical incidents still alert promptly, even while a Goal remains active.
- Suppression of one interim turn does not clear unrelated existing unread items or genuine pending input elsewhere.
- The same result holds with multiple active tasks and when the app is focused, unfocused or minimised, including transitions between turns.
- Existing builds continue without being cancelled or restarted. The solution must not require global muting, database edits, a polling watchdog, custom automation markup, or fake questions to announce completion.

### Additional information

Read-only inspection of the installed client suggests the skipped-completion display/native-notification filter and the unread-to-taskbar path use different decisions. The ordinary unread path appears to depend on live Goal/stream/ownership/pending-input or steering state without the same skipped-completion check; the taskbar badge is derived from unread counts. This is a diagnostic hypothesis, not a confirmed race condition or live proof of a patch.

Related: #22117 (closed, incomplete Goal turn notifications) and #52950 (CLI Stop hooks at continuation boundaries). This report concerns the Windows desktop app's complete attention behaviour, including unread and taskbar state.

The current workaround is partial. Clearing unread once is not prevention, and disabling all completion notifications would remove alerts the user needs. Please investigate the divergent attention paths and provide a supported unified fix with regression coverage for the acceptance criteria above.

This report is sanitised: no private project names, session IDs, local paths, raw conversation history, credentials or raw logs are attached. No installed application files were patched and no running builds were interrupted for this submission.

items.body:
### Summary

In the Windows ChatGPT/Codex desktop app, OAuth authentication through **Settings > Plugins > MCPs** succeeds and the existing MCP tools work in a local Codex chat. A dot's hosted/delegated tasks still fail to initialize the same configured MCP servers with `Auth required, when send initialize request`.

This was reproduced with two independent services: a custom Open Brain server (`openbrain`) and `nates-library`. Reauthentication, fresh delegated tasks, and exiting/restarting the desktop app did not resolve the hosted-task failure.

### Environment

- Observed: October 13, 2026, America/Los_Angeles (PDT).
- Windows version reported by the OS: `10.0.26200.0`.
- Installed Windows package: `OpenAI.Codex 26.1007.2314.0`.
- Separately installed CLI: `codex-cli 0.149.1`; this is not a measurement of the app's bundled or hosted runtime version.
- Working path: local Codex chat; desktop logs identify `hostId=local`.
- Failing path: dot-created hosted/delegated tasks with local computer access; desktop logs identify `hostId=durable`.
- Transport: Streamable HTTP, OAuth. The custom server has no static bearer-token/header override in its local configuration; MCP OAuth credential-store preference is unset/default.

### Observed reproduction sequence

1. Use an existing OAuth-protected HTTP MCP in the shared **Settings > Plugins > MCPs** screen.
2. Select Authenticate and complete the browser authorization.
3. Verify an actual read-only tool call from a local Codex chat succeeds.
4. Ask the dot to use the same existing MCP connection through a delegated task.
5. Initialization fails before tools can be called, with the error below.
6. Retry through a fresh delegated task and after exiting/restarting the desktop app: failure persists.
7. Authenticate again in the shared settings and verify local tool access again: the hosted task still fails.
8. Try the independent `nates-library` MCP through the dot: the user reports the same authentication error. A local `list_guides(limit=1)` call succeeds.

This is an observed sequence on the affected installation, not a claim that every installation reproduces it.

### Actual error

```text
resources/list failed: failed to get client: MCP startup failed: handshaking with MCP server failed: Send message error Transport [codex_rmcp_client::event_notification_transport::EventNotificationTransport<rmcp::transport::worker::WorkerTransport<rmcp::transport::streamable_http_client::StreamableHttpClientWorker<codex_rmcp_client::http_client_adapter::StreamableHttpClientAdapter>>>] error: Auth required, when send initialize request
```

### Verification and timeline

- 15:10:20 UTC: custom MCP sign-in completed; local tools subsequently worked.
- Around 15:15 UTC: a fresh dot-created task failed initialization, before that access token's one-hour expiry.
- Around 16:01–16:03 UTC: after the user restarted the app, local MCP initialization succeeded; the hosted retry still failed.
- 16:48:44 UTC: the user authenticated again. Desktop logs recorded OAuth completion and `hostId=local` Open Brain startup status `ready`; an actual local `list_projects(limit=1)` read succeeded.
- 17:01:16–17:01:28 UTC: the existing hosted task's latest Open Brain retry still failed with the error above.
- Around 17:27 UTC: a local `nates-library` `list_guides(limit=1)` read succeeded after the user reported the same hosted authentication failure for that provider.
- Hosted startup logs also showed failures for `supabase-personal-readonly` and `nates-library`. Supabase's exact error was not separately verified.

### Expected behavior

An authenticated existing connection should either be usable by the dot's supported execution path, or the app should provide an actionable authentication flow/explanation for that path. Successful authentication in the shared MCP settings should not leave the user repeatedly retrying an inaccessible connection with only a generic initialization error.

### Investigation limits and related findings

Credential availability or propagation between the local and hosted paths is a hypothesis, not a proven root cause. The hosted error names `EventNotificationTransport`; no OAuth `AuthClient` wrapper appears in that particular trace. This alone does not prove whether an Authorization header was sent. Existing custom-server logs show HTTP 401 responses but do not record credential/header presence.

The custom server initially had a separate discovery-scope mismatch, which was corrected before these successful local sign-ins. The independent provider failure supports investigating the client execution/authentication paths beyond that server-specific issue.

A separate, later local incident involved a successful token refresh followed by HTTP 400 responses and an inactive grant, consistent with refresh-token reuse detection. It cannot explain the hosted failure that began before access-token expiry. No root cause is asserted for that separate incident.

Related issue: #14144 concerns stale OAuth credentials after reauthentication. This report differs because the hosted path remains unusable after fresh tasks and a desktop restart while the local path works.

Please check how the hosted/delegated MCP client resolves credentials for connections authenticated through the shared desktop MCP settings.

No tokens, authorization URLs/codes, account IDs, private hostnames, private record contents, raw transcripts, or full logs are included.

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

codex-cli 0.162.1 (npm `@openai/codex`)

### What subscription do you have?

Not relevant: reproduces with a placeholder API key, before any request is made.

### Which model were you using?

Not relevant (startup).

### What platform is your computer?

Linux x86_64, inside a Docker container (`node:24-trixie`, Debian 13, bubblewrap 0.12.0) on an Ubuntu host with kernel 6.8. Docker's default seccomp profile, so `unshare -Ur true` fails with "Operation not permitted".

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

tmux

### What issue are you seeing?

Codex runs in a container that is itself the sandbox, so it is started with `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` and never uses bubblewrap. Every session still reports a startup warning:

```
⚠ 1 warning · f2 to view

Warnings · 1 of 1 · Startup
Codex's Linux sandbox uses bubblewrap and needs access to create user namespaces.
```

`/status` in the same session shows `Permissions: Full Access` and `Server: Local background server`.

The warning depends on how the session reaches the server, not on the session's permissions:

| Command | Server | Warning |
|---|---|---|
| `codex` | Local background server | yes (expected) |
| `codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` | Local background server | **yes** |
| `codex --no-daemon --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` | embedded | no |
| `codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` with `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"` in `config.toml` | Local background server | no |

So it looks like the shared background server checks bubblewrap once, with the sandbox mode from `config.toml`, and reports the result to every session it serves, without considering the permissions the session was started with.

The only ways to avoid it are `--no-daemon`, which gives up the shared server, or setting `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"` in `config.toml`, which also changes plain `codex` started later.

This looks like the case #15282 fixed for the earlier "could not find system bubblewrap" warning ("show it only when sandboxing is enabled"), coming back through the shared background server. #48681 reports the same message, but with a different cause (nested bubblewrap under AppArmor).

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

```bash
docker run --rm -it node:24-trixie bash

# in the container, as root
apt-get update && apt-get install -y bubblewrap git
npm install -g @openai/codex@0.162.1
su node
cd ~ && mkdir w && cd w && git init
printf 'sk-placeholder\n' | codex login --with-api-key
codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox
```

The status bar shows `⚠ 1 warning · f2 to view`; F2 shows the bubblewrap message; `/status` shows `Full Access` on the `Local background server`.

`codex --no-daemon --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` in a fresh container shows no warning.

### What is the expected behavior?

No bubblewrap warning in a session that does not use Codex's sandbox (`--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, or `danger-full-access`), whether it runs embedded or through the shared background server.

### Additional information

Started with the plain `codex`, the warning is correct: Codex's sandbox cannot run in this container.

items.body:
### What version of Codex are you using?

Codex CLI 0.160.0. The code below is unchanged at `rust-v0.162.1`.

### What issue are you seeing?

A thread that was started under one `model_provider` cannot be continued under another one. The first turn after the switch fails with `invalid_encrypted_content`.

Codex asks every provider for `reasoning.encrypted_content` and replays the stored reasoning items as they are. Encrypted reasoning can only be read by the backend that created it. So when a thread made through a gateway (a custom Responses provider in `config.toml`) is resumed on the default `openai` provider, the new backend rejects the old reasoning items and the turn fails.

### Steps

1. Add a custom Responses provider in `config.toml` (for example a gateway in front of OpenAI models) and set `model_provider` to it.
2. Run a turn that reasons: `codex exec "think step by step: how many primes are below 200?"`.
3. Set `model_provider` back to the default and run `codex resume <id>` with that thread's id. Send any prompt.
4. The turn fails with `invalid_encrypted_content`.

### Expected

The thread continues. Losing the hidden reasoning of past turns is fine; losing the thread is not.

### Where

* Every request includes `reasoning.encrypted_content`: [`client.rs#L961`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/092d3acd6bec3e3a14bdc7e7a2810ab628ab759d/codex-rs/core/src/client.rs#L961).
* Stored `Reasoning` items keep `encrypted_content` with no record of which provider created it: [`models.rs#L1050`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/092d3acd6bec3e3a14bdc7e7a2810ab628ab759d/codex-rs/protocol/src/models.rs#L1050).
* There is already a precedent: for non-OpenAI providers, Codex clears `encrypted_function_args` before it sends the history ([`client.rs#L942`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/092d3acd6bec3e3a14bdc7e7a2810ab628ab759d/codex-rs/core/src/client.rs#L942)). Reasoning `encrypted_content` gets no such treatment.

### Proposal

Either of these would fix it, and neither changes a thread that stays on one provider:

1. Record the provider on each reasoning item, and drop `encrypted_content` (keep the summary) when the history is sent to a different provider.
2. When a request fails with `invalid_encrypted_content`, retry it once without `encrypted_content` on the past reasoning items.

### Additional information

This pairs with #53234: once resume lists threads from every provider, users will pick threads from another provider, and those threads should then continue instead of failing.
